command: This directory is an OpenClaw plugin, not a standalone MCP server. OpenClaw loads it in-process inside the agent gateway with the gateway's full permissions: filesystem, network, environment variables, stored credentials and conversation transcripts. Tools registered with api.registerTool are exposed to the model exactly like MCP tools (their names, descriptions and results reach the model). Hooks such as before_prompt_build can read and rewrite prompts and messages. registerHttpRoute exposes HTTP endpoints on the gateway. Audit it as an agent tool server running with those permissions. Prioritize malicious or deceptive behavior: credential or data exfiltration, tool poisoning or hidden instructions in tool descriptions or results, prompt injection, remote code download or execution, obfuscated payloads, persistence, backdoors or unauthenticated control endpoints, and behavior that is not declared in openclaw.plugin.json or package.json. Third-party dependencies (node_modules) were removed and are out of scope. The whole plugin artifact is in scope, not only its MCP-style tools: also audit embedded skills (SKILL.md files and the instructions, references and scripts they ship), hooks, tool and HTTP route handlers, install or lifecycle scripts, and compiled or bundled code such as dist/ and build/ output. Read the entry points named in package.json and openclaw.plugin.json even when they are compiled. No shell is available: use read_file, read_file_chunk (for any file longer than one read_file result) and search_files.

shortDescription.text: Credential theft and secret leakage, e.g. hardcoded keys, env var leaks, mcp.json credential theft
Overly broad tool permissions granting agents unnecessary system control or data access
Legitimate MCP tools tampered or injected with malicious logic, returning false/biased results to manipulate the model
Dependency tampering, malicious third-party MCP servers, or backdoors in build scripts
Agent constructs and executes system commands, shell scripts, or API calls from untrusted input
Malicious instructions injected via context (OCR, web content) to hijack model control flow
MCP server or tools fail to validate identity, enabling cross-agent/cross-user unauthorized operations
No tamper-proof logging of tool calls and context changes, hindering security traceability
Unauthorized MCP instances with default configurations or lacking security compliance
Sensitive context shared across sessions or agents, causing information leakage or logic interference
Malicious tool registered with a name similar to a common tool, tricking agents into wrong calls
Malicious MCP service terminates or changes behavior after gaining trust, causing DoS or data loss
Overriding legitimate tool behavior by redefining a same-named tool
Security issues not covered by the MCP01-MCP10 classification
